subtype: Holding arms close to the body [Expressing]
passage: The wedding hall in Amritsar was loud, packed with aunties and drums, and the lights kept flickering. Shankar, five, kept his arms pressed tight to his sides, and stayed half behind his father Lokesh's leg. A relative bent down. "Come, give me a hug!" Shankar leaned away. Lokesh said easily, "He needs a minute, ji. He's warming up." After some time, Shankar was standing at the edge of the dance floor, his arms slowly loosening, watching the dhol player.

qa.q: Where was the wedding held?
qa.a: It was held in a hall in Amritsar.

qa.q: What might Shankar have been feeling with his arms pressed tight to his sides?
qa.a: He was probably cautious and a bit overwhelmed by the noisy crowd of new people. He could also have been just tired.

qa.q: How did Lokesh help Shankar?
qa.a: He stayed close, explained that Shankar needed a minute and didn't push a hug, so Shankar could warm up at his own pace.

qa.q: How might the relative feel when Shankar leans away?
qa.a: They may feel a little rebuffed, but Lokesh's easy words help them see it as shyness and not rudeness.

grounding: A shy child tucks his arms to his body around new people, and time with a familiar adult nearby helps.

subtype: Holding arms close to the body [Expressing]
passage: Pradeep's cousin Siddharth had just moved to Bhopal, and on his first day at the new school, the class teacher led him in. Siddharth, six, kept his arms tucked against his ribs and looked at the floor. "This is Siddharth," said the teacher. The class said, "Hello!" He gave the smallest nod. Pradeep, sitting nearby, saved him a seat and didn't say much. By break time Siddharth was holding a pencil box with both hands, arms a little looser, and asked Pradeep, "Which game do you play?"

qa.q: What did Pradeep do for Siddharth?
qa.a: He saved him a seat and didn't say much.

qa.q: What does Siddharth's tucked arms and lowered gaze suggest about how he feels?
qa.a: They suggest he feels cautious and shy among new people. He could also just be feeling tired from the move.

qa.q: What could the teacher do to help Siddharth settle in?
qa.a: The teacher can let him stay near Pradeep and give him time before asking him to speak or perform.

qa.q: How might Pradeep see Siddharth's behaviour on his first morning?
qa.a: He may see a quiet new boy who needs a friendly face, and he responds by sitting close.

grounding: A shy child keeps his arms tucked around new people, and time with a familiar person helps.

passage:
Day one: at the school gate in Ranchi, Ojas, four, clenched both fists and stamped when his mother Trisha said no to the toy stall. She knelt. "Your hands look angry. Want to tell me?" He shouted "Toy!" and she said, "You're frustrated."
Day three: Ojas's fists tightened when his block tower fell. Trisha handed him a soft ball and he squeezed it hard.
Day six: he held up his fists and said, "Angry hands, Amma!" then squeezed the ball.

qa.q: What did Ojas shout when his mother said no to the toy stall?
qa.a: He shouted "Toy!"

qa.q: What was Ojas feeling when his fists tightened on day three?
qa.a: He was frustrated or angry that his tower fell, and squeezing the soft ball gave that feeling somewhere to go. He might also have been disappointed after all his careful stacking.

qa.q: What worked well in how Trisha helped Ojas across the days?
qa.a: She gave him words for the feeling and a safe outlet, the soft ball, so that by day six he named it himself.

qa.q: How might Trisha feel on day six when Ojas says, "Angry hands, Amma!"?
qa.a: Trisha is probably pleased and proud that Ojas can now name his feeling and reach for the ball himself.

grounding: A preschooler clenches his fists in anger, and adults offer words for the feeling and a safe outlet such as a soft ball.

passage: The generator had stopped mid-lesson at the tuition class in Nashik, and the room was hot and dim. Ankita, five, was struggling to tie her shoelace, her tongue between her teeth. It slipped again. Her fists clenched and her face went red. Her teacher Jyoti crouched beside her. "Those are strong fists. That knot is being stubborn." She handed Ankita a squishy ball from the shelf. Ankita squeezed it twice, breathed out, and tried the lace again.

qa.q: What was Ankita trying to tie?
qa.a: She was trying to tie her shoelace.

qa.q: What does Ankita's clenched fists and red face suggest she felt, and what else might have added to it?
qa.a: They suggest anger and frustration at the slipping lace. The hot, dim room may have made her feel worse.

qa.q: What could Jyoti try when Ankita gets frustrated again?
qa.a: She can keep offering a squishy ball or another safe outlet and use words such as "stubborn" for the knot.

qa.q: How might Ankita feel when Jyoti calls the knot stubborn?
qa.a: She may feel that her teacher is on her side, and the problem is the knot, not her.

grounding: A preschooler clenches her fists in frustration, and a teacher offers words and a safe outlet.

passage: Note from Ms Noor, Reception teacher. During carpet time on Tuesday, Hafsa drummed her fingers on her knees and swayed. I was about to say, "Sit still," but I noticed she could repeat every line of the story when I asked. On Thursday, during a long assembly, she drummed and kept looking at the door; then she wandered off. So the same fidgeting seemed to mean focus on Tuesday and boredom on Thursday. I now check the context first.

qa.q: What did Hafsa do with her fingers on Tuesday?
qa.a: She drummed her fingers on her knees.

qa.q: What did Hafsa's fidgeting seem to show on Tuesday versus Thursday, according to Ms Noor?
qa.a: On Tuesday it seemed to be focus, because she could repeat the story. On Thursday it looked like boredom, since she looked at the door and wandered off.

qa.q: What could Ms Noor do to avoid scolding unfairly?
qa.a: She can look at the setting and what Hafsa is doing before telling her to sit still, and let her fidget when she is listening.

qa.q: How might Hafsa feel if she were told off on Tuesday for fidgeting?
qa.a: She might feel confused or unfairly blamed, since she was actually listening carefully.

grounding: Fidgeting can come from energy, focus or boredom, and context prevents unfair scolding.

passage: At the panchayat school in a hill village, Gurpreet's four-year-old, Nirmala, sat in the second row drumming the desk with two fingers during the maths story. She tapped, then hummed, then tapped again. A visitor whispered, "That child isn't paying attention." The teacher shook her head. "Ask her what happened in the story." Nirmala looked up and said, "The goat ate five roti and then he was full." The visitor blinked. Nirmala went back to tapping.

qa.q: How many roti did the goat eat in Nirmala's answer?
qa.a: The goat ate five roti.

qa.q: What might Nirmala's drumming and humming suggest about how she was thinking, and what else could it show?
qa.a: It seems to help her concentrate, since she could retell the story exactly. It might also have been extra energy she needed to let out.

qa.q: What could the visitor do differently next time?
qa.a: The visitor could check what the child is doing and ask before deciding the child is not paying attention.

qa.q: How might the teacher see Nirmala's tapping compared with the visitor?
qa.a: The teacher knows that Nirmala listens while she taps, so she is not bothered, whereas the visitor took it as a sign of not listening.

grounding: A child drums her fingers from energy or focus, and checking the context prevents an unfair scolding.

passage: At the flat's play area in Lucknow, Jahnavi held up her hand with two fingers crossed and whispered to Rafiq, "If I cross fingers, it's for luck. Do it too!" Rafiq crossed his, and the two waited beside the sandpit for the ice-cream van. When it rang its bell, they hugged. Next day Jahnavi made a different sign, a thumb tucked behind a fist. "That's our secret sign," she said. "It means come to the swing." Rafiq grinned and tucked his thumb too.

qa.q: What did Jahnavi do with her fingers to bring luck?
qa.a: She crossed two fingers.

qa.q: What is Rafiq probably feeling when he copies the signs?
qa.a: He likely feels included and excited to share a secret with Jahnavi, since he grinned and copied at once. He might also just enjoy copying.

qa.q: What could an adult do when children invent secret signs?
qa.a: They can enjoy the game and remember it's playful, while reminding children to tell them about anything that makes them uneasy.

qa.q: How might another child who doesn't know the signs feel?
qa.a: They might feel left out or puzzled, since the secret signs only work for those who share them.

grounding: Crossed fingers and secret signs are playful conventions that only work within a shared group.

passage:
"Promise you won't tell," said Farhan, holding up crossed fingers behind his back.
"What's that?" asked Ganga.
"It's a promise sign. Kids at my old school did it."
"We do a pinky."
"That's different!"
"It's the same," said Ganga. "It just looks different."
They grinned. "Okay," said Farhan, and showed his pinky too. "Ready? Let's hide the ball and see if Papa finds it."

qa.q: What sign did Farhan hold up behind his back?
qa.a: He held up crossed fingers behind his back.

qa.q: What does Ganga seem to think about the different signs?
qa.a: Ganga thinks they mean the same promise even though they look different, and the grin shows Ganga is happy about it. Farhan may feel unsure at first because his sign is the one he knows.

qa.q: What would help children who use different signs?
qa.a: They can explain their signs and choose one for the game together, as Farhan and Ganga did.

qa.q: How might Farhan see the pinky compared with his crossed fingers?
qa.a: He might find it new and interesting, showing that groups have their own signs.

grounding: Crossed fingers and pinky promises are playful conventions that vary by group.

passage: Home-visit note by Sangeeta, anganwadi worker. Gopika, five, folded her hands in namaste when I came in and said, "Namaste, Sangeeta-didi." Her grandmother told me that they do not insist on it. Instead, everyone greets each other this way each morning, and Gopika started copying it a few months ago. When I gave her a biscuit she put her hand over her heart, smiling. I noted that respect seems to be growing from warmth and repetition, not from being told to do it.

qa.q: What did Gopika say when she folded her hands?
qa.a: She said, "Namaste, Sangeeta-didi."

qa.q: What might Gopika be feeling when she places her hand over her heart after getting the biscuit?
qa.a: She seems to feel thankful and happy, since she is smiling. She could also simply be copying what she sees others do.

qa.q: What could families do to help children learn respectful greetings?
qa.a: They can greet each other warmly every day and let children copy at their own pace, as Gopika's family does.

qa.q: How does Gopika's grandmother see it?
qa.a: She sees that Gopika has learned to greet people because the family does it daily, and not because she was forced.

grounding: A preschooler folds her hands in namaste or places a hand over the heart to greet or thank, learned through warm modelling.

passage: At the village's temple courtyard, Madhav, four, saw the elderly priest and pressed his palms together, saying "Namaste, Baba." He had watched his father Shankar do the same every evening. The priest smiled and touched his head lightly, and Madhav giggled. Shankar hadn't told him to do it. Later a small boy from another village just waved. Shankar only smiled at both, and said, "Everyone has a way to say hello."

qa.q: Where did Madhav greet the priest?
qa.a: He greeted the priest in the temple courtyard.

qa.q: What might Madhav have been feeling when the priest touched his head?
qa.a: He probably felt happy and welcomed, since he giggled. He might also have felt a little shy.

qa.q: What could Shankar do if Madhav didn't want to fold his hands one evening?
qa.a: He can keep greeting people warmly himself and let Madhav join in when he wants.

qa.q: How might the priest see Madhav's namaste?
qa.a: The priest may see a small child showing respect and warmth, and answered with a smile and a gentle touch.

grounding: A preschooler folds his hands in namaste as respect learned through modelling, without being forced.

passage: The baby had finally fallen asleep on the sofa after a night of crying, and the neighbours' drill had just started next door. Deepika, five, was about to shout when her aunt Farida raised a finger to her lips and looked at the baby. Deepika froze, and then glanced at Farida's face, which was soft, not stern. She put her own finger to her lips and tiptoed to her colouring book. She whispered, "Shh. Baby's sleeping."

qa.q: Why did Farida raise a finger to her lips?
qa.a: She wanted quiet because the baby had finally fallen asleep on the sofa.

qa.q: What did Deepika read from Farida's face, and what did it lead her to think?
qa.a: She saw that it was soft and not stern, so she understood the gesture as a request for quiet and not as being in trouble. She could have thought she was being scolded if the face had been hard.

qa.q: What could Farida do to help Deepika understand this gesture in other places?
qa.a: She can show the same gesture in the library or at bedtime, and say quietly what it means.

qa.q: How might Farida feel when Deepika tiptoes away?
qa.a: She may feel relieved and grateful that the baby's sleep is safe, and proud of Deepika.

grounding: A preschooler reads a finger to the lips as a request for quiet, and the adult's face shows she is not in trouble.

passage: In the library in Manchester, Francis, six, whispered a question. His uncle Samir put a finger to his lips and smiled. "Yes, in the library we use quiet voices." Francis wasn't sure. "Am I in trouble?" Samir shook his head. "No, look at my face. I'm not cross. The finger just means quiet here." Francis relaxed, put his own finger to his lips and picked a book about trains.

qa.q: Where were Francis and Samir?
qa.a: They were in the library in Manchester.

qa.q: What worried Francis about Samir's finger to his lips?
qa.a: He was afraid he might be in trouble, since he asked. Samir's smile and words showed that it just meant a quiet voice.

qa.q: How could Samir help if Francis sees the same gesture at a friend's house?
qa.a: He can explain that the setting decides its meaning, and that a calm face shows it isn't a scolding.

qa.q: How might the other people in the library see Francis's whisper?
qa.a: They probably barely notice it, since it was already a whisper, and the gesture was gentle.

grounding: A finger to the lips means quiet in a library, and the adult's smile shows the child isn't in trouble.

passage: In the one-room school at the edge of a village near Jaipur, Jasleen, five, waved her hand high with her tongue between her teeth. Teacher Rajni was writing on the board and didn't turn. Jasleen's arm began to shake. She almost blurted out, "Miss, Miss!" Then Rajni glanced over and gave a small nod. Jasleen let out her breath and lowered her hand. "Miss, can I go to the toilet?" Rajni nodded, "Go," and Jasleen ran.

qa.q: What did Jasleen ask when Rajni nodded?
qa.a: She asked, "Miss, can I go to the toilet?"

qa.q: What might Jasleen have been feeling while she waited with her hand raised?
qa.a: She was probably restless and anxious, since her arm shook and she nearly blurted out. The nod may have brought her some relief.

qa.q: What could a teacher do to help children wait for a turn?
qa.a: They can give a quick nod or a look to show they have seen the raised hand, even if they can't call on the child yet.

qa.q: How does Rajni see the raised hand while she writes?
qa.a: Rajni might not notice at first because of being busy, but a quick glance and nod lets Jasleen know she is seen.

grounding: A child learns to raise a hand and wait, and a quick nod from the teacher eases her impatience.

passage: In a Warsaw primary school, Marek's hand shot up. "I know! I know!" whispered Marek. Teacher Santiago was helping another child and held up one finger. Marek bounced on his toes, chewing his sleeve, then his hand went up and down. Santiago nodded at him. Marek sat, and when the other child finished, Santiago said, "Marek?" He gave the answer in a rush, cheeks flushed. "Well waited," said Santiago.

qa.q: How did Marek's teacher tell him to wait?
qa.a: Santiago held up one finger.

qa.q: What might Marek have been feeling as he bounced on his toes and chewed his sleeve?
qa.a: He seemed excited and impatient to share his answer, and waiting was hard for him. He might also have been afraid of forgetting it.

qa.q: What could help Marek wait more easily next time?
qa.a: A quick nod from the teacher, as Santiago gave, or a signal that his turn is coming would help.

qa.q: How might the other child helped by Santiago feel while Marek fidgets?
qa.a: That child might feel hurried, so a clear promise to Marek that his turn is next helps both children.

grounding: A child raises a hand to speak and waiting is hard, so the teacher's nod eases frustration.

passage: By the cowshed in their village, Yash, four, pretended to be a bird. He flapped his arms, ran round the haystack and made a beak with his fingers. His grandmother Aadhya, shelling peas, asked, "Are you a crow or a parrot?" He looked at her, shy, and kept flapping. She guessed. "A parrot! Green wings." He grinned. Then he cupped his hands to his mouth and made a drinking gesture. "You want water, little bird?" Yash nodded and she brought a cup.

qa.q: What did Yash pretend to be by the cowshed?
qa.a: He pretended to be a bird.

qa.q: What does Yash's grin and his switching to a drinking gesture suggest he was thinking?
qa.a: He seems happy that his grandmother understood his pretend play, and used mime for the water because words felt hard for him with shyness. He might also simply have been thirsty.

qa.q: What could Aadhya do to help Yash use words when he's ready?
qa.a: She can keep guessing playfully and sometimes offer a word for what he mimed, without pressing him to speak.

qa.q: How might Aadhya feel as she guesses what Yash is miming?
qa.a: She may feel amused and close to him, enjoying the game while working out what he needs.

grounding: A preschooler mimes being a bird and drinking, and a shy child relies on the adult to guess.

passage: On a beach in Lagos, Emeka, five, held his hands like a steering wheel and made engine noises. His friend Wei, not sure what Emeka was doing, stared at him. Emeka waved a hand for Wei to come closer, turned an imaginary wheel and honked with the flat of his hand. "Oh! You're driving!" said Wei. Emeka nodded and pointed at the empty sand beside him. Wei climbed into the invisible car. They drove past the ice-cream stall and stopped for an imaginary fuel fill-up.

qa.q: What did Emeka use his hands to be?
qa.a: He held his hands like a steering wheel.

qa.q: What did Emeka seem to want when he pointed at the empty sand?
qa.a: He wanted Wei to join him in the pretend car, and he used gestures because his first try wasn't understood. He might also have wanted to show off his idea.

qa.q: How could Wei help a friend whose mime Wei doesn't understand at first?
qa.a: Wei can keep watching and guess, as before, and ask questions like "Are you driving?"

qa.q: How might Wei have felt when he first couldn't work out the mime?
qa.a: Wei may have felt puzzled, and then pleased and included once the mime made sense.

grounding: A preschooler mimes driving and the friend has to guess, showing imagination and the limits of gesture without words.

passage: At the fish market in Osaka, Aiko, five, held her arms wide. "The fish was THIS big!" she told her friend Yuki, who was the same age. "It was bigger than Papa's suitcase!" Yuki wasn't sure. "How many fish?" Aiko held up three fingers, then five, then changed her mind and counted again on her fingers, whispering numbers. "Three! No, four." Her father laughed quietly behind her. Yuki nodded, believing every word, and spread her own arms wide to show her own fish.

qa.q: How many fish did Aiko finally say she saw?
qa.a: She finally said four fish.

qa.q: What does Aiko's wide arms and changing counts suggest about her feeling?
qa.a: They suggest excitement about the fish, so she stretched the size, not that she meant to mislead. She may also have been unsure of the number.

qa.q: What could Aiko's father do next time she describes something big?
qa.a: He can enjoy the story and ask gentle questions to help her count and compare, without correcting her excitement.

qa.q: How does Yuki seem to take Aiko's story?
qa.a: She believes it and matches it with her own arms, which shows how gestures can carry size before children can measure.

grounding: A child shows size and number with gestures that exaggerate for excitement, before she can measure.

passage: Nursery room note by Preeti. Today at circle time I asked the children how old they were. Jagdish, four, held up four fingers proudly, and then held up five when Riya said she was five. "Me too!" I asked how many biscuits he ate and he held both hands wide and said, "A hundred!" He wasn't trying to fool anyone; he looked delighted. Gestures like these carry numbers before exact counting is learned. I counted with him, using fingers, and he grinned at seeing it was six.

qa.q: How many fingers did Jagdish hold up for his age at first?
qa.a: He held up four fingers.

qa.q: What might Jagdish have been feeling when he said "A hundred!" with both hands wide?
qa.a: He seemed excited and proud about the biscuits, and the number showed how much they meant to him and not an exact count. He might also have wanted to match Riya.

qa.q: How can Preeti help Jagdish with real counting without dampening his joy?
qa.a: She can count with him using fingers and celebrate the real number, as Preeti did.

qa.q: How might Riya see Jagdish's number?
qa.a: She may take it seriously, or she might see he wants to match her, since he changed his fingers to five.

grounding: A child uses finger and arm gestures for number and size, exaggerating from excitement rather than accuracy.

passage: Note from Trisha, Class 1 teacher at an after-school centre. At pick-up time, Deepika, six, was teased about her red lunch box by two classmates. She went to the corner of the reading sofa, pulled her knees to her chest and tucked her chin in. I sat a little way off and read my own book, near but not looking. After a while I said, "I'm here if you want." She didn't answer for a while, then leaned toward me and whispered, "They laughed."

qa.q: What did the classmates tease Deepika about?
qa.a: They teased her about her red lunch box.

qa.q: What might Deepika have been feeling when she pulled her knees to her chest and tucked her chin in?
qa.a: She was probably hurt and ashamed and wanted to hide. She might also have simply needed a quiet moment.

qa.q: Why did Trisha sit a little way off and read her own book?
qa.a: Trisha wanted to give Deepika a quiet presence without asking many questions, which let Deepika speak when she was ready.

qa.q: How might the classmates see Deepika's curling up?
qa.a: They might not realise how much the teasing hurt her, which is why an adult noticing matters.

grounding: A child curls up after being teased, and a quiet, non-intrusive presence works better than many questions.

passage: I am Baljeet, and at our after-school club I saw Lokesh, a classmate, sit on the beanbag with his shoulders hunched and his face turned into his knees. The teacher had told him off for running in the corridor, and he had been laughing before. Now he was very quiet and pulled his sleeves over his hands. Nobody spoke to him. After a while the club helper sat on the floor nearby with a picture book. I can't tell what Lokesh was feeling, maybe sad or ashamed.

qa.q: What had the teacher told Lokesh off for?
qa.a: The teacher had told him off for running in the corridor.

qa.q: What might Lokesh have been feeling as he hunched his shoulders and pulled his sleeves over his hands?
qa.a: He may have been sad or ashamed after being told off and wanted to hide. He might also have been tired after running about.

qa.q: What could the club helper do next if Lokesh stays curled up?
qa.a: The helper can stay nearby quietly, keep the picture book handy and let Lokesh come over when ready.

qa.q: How might Baljeet's view of Lokesh differ from the helper's?
qa.a: Baljeet only sees Lokesh being quiet and can't tell why, whereas the helper knows what happened earlier.

grounding: A child curls into himself after a scolding, and an observer can only guess at the feeling.
